./research/pathway_additions/2026-10-11-next-201/sulfoquinovose-source-projection.json:578:      "comment": "<a href=\"/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10247\">Sulfoquinovose</a> is a major component of organo-sulfur compounds in nature [<a href=\"http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/428677\">Harwood79</a>].  It is synthesized by higher plants, mosses, ferns, algae and most photosynthetic bacteria and serves as the polar headgroup of the sulfolipid in photosynthetic membranes [<a href=\"http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15012227\">Benning98</a>, <a href=\"http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17334828\">Benning07</a>].\n<p>\nBacteria that are able to utilize sulfoquinovose as their sole source of carbon and energy for growth have been isolated. As of 2015, two degradation pathways have been described. One pathway is analogous to glycolysis (this pathway) while the other is analogous to the Entner-Doudoroff pathway (see <a href=\"/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-7722\">sulfoquinovose degradation II</a>).\n<p>\n<b>About this pathway</b>\n<p>\nIt was recently shown that <i>E. coli</i> can also utilize <a href=\"/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10247\">6-sulfo-D-quinovose</a> as its sole source of carbon and energy for growth.  The enzymes involved in this pathway were initially identified by analysis of differences in the proteomes of cultures grown with glucose vs. sulfoquinovose [<a href=\"http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24463506\">Denger14</a>].  \n<p>\n<a href=\"/gene?orgid=META&id=EG11845-MONOMER\">sulfoquinovose isomerase</a> catalyzes the initial isomerization of <a href=\"/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10247\">6-sulfo-D-quinovose</a> to <a href=\"/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-16501\">6-deoxy-6-sulfo-D-fructose</a>.  <a href=\"/gene?orgid=META&id=EG11848-MONOMER\">6-deoxy-6-sulfofructose kinase</a> phosphorylates <a href=\"/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-16501\">6-deoxy-6-sulfo-D-fructose</a> to <a href=\"/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-16502\">6-deoxy-6-sulfo-D-fructose 1-phosphate</a>, which is cleaved by <a href=\"/gene?orgid=META&id=EG11846-MONOMER\">6-deoxy-6-sulfofructose-1-phosphate aldolase</a> to form <a href=\"/compound?orgid=META&id=DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE\">glycerone phosphate</a> and <a href=\"/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=CPD-18717\">3-sulfolactaldehyde</a>.  <a href=\"/gene?orgid=META&id=EG11847-MONOMER\">3-sulfolactaldehyde reductase</a> reduces <a href=\"/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=CPD-18717\">3-sulfolactaldehyde</a> to <a href=\"/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate\" title=\"<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate''>2,3-Dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate</a> (DHPS) is a widespread intermediate in plant and algal transformations of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10247''>6-sulfo-D-quinovose</a> from the plant sulfolipid <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL''>an 6-sulfo-α-D-quinovosyl diacylglycerol</a> [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7626014''>Pugh95</a>]. It is also recovered quantitatively during bacterial degradation of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10247''>6-sulfo-D-quinovose</a> [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14602597''>Roy03</a>], and is secreted by all diatoms [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5085579''>Benson72</a>].\t

DHPS is also a putative precursor of <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=CPD-11797''>2-<i>O</i>-sulfonatolactate</a> in some organisms, such as <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-246200''><i>Ruegeria pomeroyi</i> DSS-3</a> [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20150239''>Mayer10</a>].\">3-sulfopropanediol</a> (DHPS) in an NADH-dependent reaction. \n<p>\nThe final products of this pathway are <a href=\"/compound?orgid=META&id=DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE\">glycerone phosphate</a>, which powers the cell via <a href=\"/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=GLYCOLYSIS\">glycolysis I (from glucose 6-phosphate)</a>, and <a href=\"/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate\" title=\"<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate''>2,3-Dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate</a> (DHPS) is a widespread intermediate in plant and algal transformations of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10247''>6-sulfo-D-quinovose</a> from the plant sulfolipid <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL''>an 6-sulfo-α-D-quinovosyl diacylglycerol</a> [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7626014''>Pugh95</a>]. It is also recovered quantitatively during bacterial degradation of <a href=''/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10247''>6-sulfo-D-quinovose</a> [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14602597''>Roy03</a>], and is secreted by all diatoms [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5085579''>Benson72</a>].\t

DHPS is also a putative precursor of <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=CPD-11797''>2-<i>O</i>-sulfonatolactate</a> in some organisms, such as <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-246200''><i>Ruegeria pomeroyi</i> DSS-3</a> [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20150239''>Mayer10</a>].\">DHPS</a>, which is excreted and can be further degraded by other bacteria.",

"comment": "Sulfoquinovose is a major component of organo-sulfur compounds in nature [Harwood79]. It is synthesized by higher plants, mosses, ferns, algae and most photosynthetic bacteria and serves as the polar headgroup of the sulfolipid in photosynthetic membranes [Benning98, Benning07].

Bacteria that are able to utilize sulfoquinovose as their sole source of carbon and energy for growth have been isolated. As of 2015, two degradation pathways have been described. One pathway is analogous to glycolysis (this pathway) while the other is analogous to the Entner-Doudoroff pathway (see sulfoquinovose degradation II).

About this pathway

It was recently shown that E. coli can also utilize 6-sulfo-D-quinovose as its sole source of carbon and energy for growth. The enzymes involved in this pathway were initially identified by analysis of differences in the proteomes of cultures grown with glucose vs. sulfoquinovose [Denger14].

sulfoquinovose isomerase catalyzes the initial isomerization of 6-sulfo-D-quinovose to 6-deoxy-6-sulfo-D-fructose. 6-deoxy-6-sulfofructose kinase phosphorylates 6-deoxy-6-sulfo-D-fructose to 6-deoxy-6-sulfo-D-fructose 1-phosphate, which is cleaved by 6-deoxy-6-sulfofructose-1-phosphate aldolase to form glycerone phosphate and 3-sulfolactaldehyde. 3-sulfolactaldehyde reductase reduces 3-sulfolactaldehyde to 3-sulfopropanediol (DHPS) in an NADH-dependent reaction.
